newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-"FINALLY" MAY BE TOO LATE FOR HOLYFIELD-TYSON.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-"FINALLY" MAY BE TOO LATE FOR HOLYFIELD-TYSON.

text.p: Promoters have dubbed Saturday's Mike Tyson-Evander Holyfield heavyweight title fight, "Finally", but for some fans it is simply, "Too Late."

Five years ago when they originally were supposed to fight, when both men clearly were at the top of their games, there would have been great debates about the relative merits of their styles and the outcome of the battle.
But now there seems to be a more macabre interest in the outcome -- like waiting for a wreck at the Indy 500 -- mostly over questions surrounding Holyfield's health and his fading skills.

Is his heart, once diagnosed with a hole in it, okay as recent medical tests say? Isn't Holyfield an ancient 34 after taking so many punches in all those tough fights he has had? Isn't his brawler's heart his biggest drawback against a hard-driving, power-punching Tyson?

Should we believe it was only the flu that kept Holyfield from finishing Riddick Bowe when he had him all but knocked out a year ago? And what about Holyfield's inability just last May to take out an under-weight punching bag like Bobby Czyz?

That all of these questions have been raised are reason enough in the eyes of oddsmakers to make Tyson a 15-1 favourite to hold onto his World Boxing Association's heavyweight title in the MGM Grand Arena Saturday.

The card also includes Michael Moorer defending his International Boxing Federation heavyweight title against South African Francois Botha, and World Boxing Council strawweight champion Ricardo Lopez of Mexico fighting Morgan Nduma from South Africa.
Faith in God is probably Holyfield's biggest reason for thinking he can beat Tyson. And it seems no one this side of Mother Teresa has more faith than Holyfield.

The Bible-breathing fighter is on a crusade to spread the word of God, convinced God is using him as a vessel to demonstrate to the infidels, through a boxing match, the power of faith. And Holyfield is convinced that the man in the ring with the most faith in God will win.

"The fight is a blessing to me," Holyfield, who will earn $11 million, said earlier this week. "I have the opportunity ... to show just how good God is in my performance. There's no way I cannot (win), if I just trust in God. God is that good."
Tyson and Holyfield originally were scheduled to fight in 1991. But a rib injury to Tyson postponed the fight and his rape conviction cancelled it.
Tyson spent three years handing out basketballs in prison, studying his new-found Islam religion and getting tatoos.
Holyfield went on to become God's acolyte, to make a lot of money -- well over $75 million -- and to take a lot of punches.

The first clear sign that perhaps the punches were beginning to add up on Holyfield came as early as 1991 in the form of hard-punching, hard-partying, journeyman Bert Cooper, a last-minute substitute for Tyson.
Cooper knocked down Holyfield and sent him reeling around the ring like a drunken rag doll early in the fight. Somehow Holyfield survived, and went on to pummel Cooper.
But it is notable that even then Holyfield was underpowered, unable to put away Cooper when he had him hurt.

Holyfield went on to some huge wars -- most notably against Bowe and even George Foreman -- where he took some major punishment, even in victory. His ability to take a punch certainly has not improved with time.

Tyson, on the other hand, took no punches in prison, and emerged rusty, of course. But after wading through four barely warm bodies in 13 months he seems to have regained much of his timing and finesse. His power was never a question.
The 30-year-old Tyson, who will receive $30 million to fight Holyfield, also professes a strong belief in his religion. But he has taken a much quieter approach to his beliefs.
He did, however, respond to Holyfield's implications that his faith is stronger than Tyson's and therefore God will favour the challenger in the ring.
"For someone to make that statement he would have to think God wants him to win the fight," said Tyson. "What? God don't like me?"
While most people expect a victory from the 45-1 Tyson, some give Holyfield (32-3) a chance, mostly because he is one of the rare Tyson opponents who have not been knee-buckling afraid of him.

"Even though I predict that Tyson will win," said Emanuel Steward, a trainer of several former champions, "I don't see it as a mismatch, because Holyfield is up for this fight. And he's physically in shape as well as mentally, and that's what makes for great fights.
"It may be interesting to see Mike get hit a little bit."
Tyson's take on the missed 1991 opportunity and the upcoming bout is, "I don't believe he is in my league now. I don't believe he was in my league back then."
